options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Images must be sent in a fixed order, which determines how they are referenced.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Multiple images are supported and each carries a token cost proportional to its size, so a handful of large images can consume a substantial share of the window before any text is considered. Sizing them to what the task requires is the practical consequence. Ordering is preserved and all of them are read.

stem: A team wants to know whether an integration is healthy before routing traffic to it. What should the check exercise?

options.text: The application's own dependencies, which must be available for it to serve.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The reachability of the endpoint, which confirms the network is available.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The validity of the credential, which confirms requests will be accepted.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A real call through the same path the traffic will take.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: A readiness check that does not exercise the actual path passes while the path is broken: a wrong model name, an expired permission, a misconfigured gateway. A minimal real call is what makes the signal meaningful, balanced against not spending much on it. The narrower checks are components of that rather than substitutes.

stem: An integration works in development and fails in production with the same code. What is worth checking first?

options.text: The concurrency, which is higher in production than development exercised.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The configuration that differs between them, including credentials and limits.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The model version, which may not be available within the production environment.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The request payloads, which may be larger in production than in development.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Identical code behaving differently points at what is not identical, and configuration is the largest and most commonly divergent surface: keys, base addresses, quotas, environment variables. Payload size and concurrency are genuine production-only factors and are worth checking after the cheaper comparison.

stem: A prompt asks for prose and a downstream step parses it. What does moving to a structured format change about cost?

options.text: Cache reads rise, since any structured prefix is more stable than a prose one.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Input tokens fall, since the schema replaces the formatting instructions.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Output tokens fall, since the structure carries less filler than prose does.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Nothing, since the same information is conveyed either way it is expressed.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Prose spends tokens on connective language that a structured response omits, and output is the more expensive side of the bill, so the format choice has a direct cost effect on top of removing the parsing risk. Input instructions change little, and caching is unaffected by the shape of the output.

stem: A team wants to compare two prompts fairly. What must the comparison include beyond output quality?

options.text: How readable each prompt is for the people who will maintain it.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: How many attempts each required well before reaching its current form.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: How each behaves when the model version is subsequently changed.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: What each costs and how long each takes on the same set of cases.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: A prompt that is marginally better and twice the cost is not obviously the better choice, and the decision needs both numbers on the same cases. Maintainability matters and is a softer criterion, development effort is sunk, and version robustness is a separate question worth asking later.

stem: Caching is enabled on a prompt whose prefix is read roughly once per write. What follows?

options.text: The arrangement costs more than not caching, since the write premium is not recovered.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The arrangement is neutral, since one read right at the discounted rate offsets one write.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The arrangement's effect depends on the prefix length rather than the read count.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The arrangement saves money, since any read at the discounted rate is a saving.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: A write costs more than ordinary input and a read costs much less, so the break-even sits above one read per write. At roughly one-to-one the premium is paid and only partly recovered. This is why establishing the reuse pattern precedes enabling caching rather than following it.

stem: Peak demand is several times the average and the account's limits are sized to the average. What does capacity planning require?

options.text: Sizing against the median, which is less distorted by the extreme periods.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Sizing against the peak, or shaping the peak down to what is available.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Sizing against the average, and accepting rejections during the peak periods.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Sizing against the peak, and reducing the limit again once it has passed.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Limits bind at the moment demand is highest, so a system sized to its average fails exactly when it is busiest. The two available responses are to raise the ceiling or to move deferrable work off the peak. Planning against averages or medians is what produces the outage.

stem: A team reports cost per request as the metric for a workload. What can that conceal?

options.text: The split between input and output, which are billed at different rates.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The variance between requests, which an average figure does not convey.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Requests per completed task, which may have risen as cost per request fell.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Total spend, which depends on volume as well as on the cost of each request.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Optimizations that reduce the cost of an individual call frequently increase how many calls a task takes: retries, verification passes, decomposition. Measuring per completed outcome is what keeps the comparison honest. Volume, rate split and variance are all real and none of them inverts the conclusion the way this does.

stem: Reasoning effort is raised and users report the application feels slower. What is the relationship?

options.text: Reasoning is cached between requests, so only the first request is slower.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Reasoning is performed concurrently, and so it should not affect the response time.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Reasoning is excluded from the response, so it has no effect on latency.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Reasoning is generated before the answer, so it delays the first useful output.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Reasoning tokens are produced sequentially ahead of the answer, so a larger budget lengthens the wait before anything useful appears, which is what an interactive user experiences. That trade is the reason effort should be set per task class rather than globally, and why interactive paths often warrant a lower setting.

stem: A workload's usage figures show high cache creation and almost no cache reads. What does that indicate?

options.text: The cache is expiring, so entries are gone before a second request arrives.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The prefix is too short, so entries are created and immediately discarded.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The reads are being counted as ordinary input rather than as cache reads.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The prefix is varying, so each request writes a new entry nothing reads.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Writes without reads is the signature of an unstable prefix: something near the top differs per request, so every call creates an entry that never matches again. Expiry produces the same shape only when requests are far apart, which is why the traffic pattern distinguishes the two. Short prefixes create no entry at all.

stem: A workload is latency-sensitive and cost-sensitive, and the two point at different tiers. What resolves it?

options.text: Choosing the faster tier, since in fact latency is visible to users and cost is not.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Running both and routing each request to whichever responds first.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Choosing the middle tier, which is a reasonable compromise between the two.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Establishing which constraint actually binds, and optimizing the other within it.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Design decisions are made by identifying the binding constraint and treating the rest as things to optimize within it, which also makes the trade explicit for anyone reviewing the choice later. Splitting the difference obscures what was given up, and racing two tiers pays for both on every request.

stem: A team must choose between raising the model tier and raising the reasoning effort for a task that is failing. What distinguishes the two levers?

options.text: Effort is configured per account, while tier can be selected on each individual request.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Effort affects only latency, while tier is the lever that affects the quality of the answer.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Effort applies to interactive workloads, while tier selection applies to batch workloads.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Effort adds reasoning tokens per request; tier changes the model doing the reasoning.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: The two act on different things and are priced differently: more effort buys more intermediate reasoning from the same model, billed as output, while a higher tier buys a more capable model on every token. Trying the cheaper lever first, and measuring, is what keeps the decision evidence-based rather than reflexive.

stem: An orchestrator must decide how many workers to spawn for a request. What should that number follow from?

options.text: The natural divisions in the work, rather than a figure fixed in advance.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The budget allocated to the run, divided by the expected cost of each individual worker.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The throughput available on the account, so the fan-out never exceeds what it permits.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Decomposition should follow the structure of the request: a topic with three genuine subtopics does not benefit from five workers, and forcing a fixed count produces either overlap or thin coverage. Throughput and budget are ceilings the chosen number must respect rather than the thing that determines it.

stem: An orchestrator passes each worker the entire conversation so far. What does that cost?

options.text: Determinism, since each worker sees material that varies between runs.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Context and money per worker, most of it irrelevant to that worker's task.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Isolation, since workers can observe what other workers have produced.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Ordering, since in fact workers cannot be run until the conversation is complete.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: The reason to delegate is that each participant gets a focused context sized to its own task. Forwarding everything pays for the full history per worker and dilutes the instruction that matters. Constructing a specific brief for each worker is what makes the pattern economical as well as more accurate.

stem: A worker's brief is written in general terms and results vary widely between workers. What should change?

options.text: The model tier, which should be raised so the general brief is interpreted better.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The brief, which should state what this worker must produce and in what form.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The aggregation, which should reconcile the variation after the results arrive.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The worker count, which should be reduced so the variation is less visible.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Variation between workers given the same vague instruction is the instruction's doing, and specifying the output shape and scope is what makes results comparable and combinable. Raising the tier makes each interpretation better without making them consistent, and reconciling afterwards is repair work for a preventable problem.

stem: A run must not exceed a cost ceiling however many steps it takes. What enforces that?

options.text: A budget tracked across the run, checked before each further call.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: A limit on iterations, which bounds how many calls the run can make.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A timeout on the run, which bounds how long it may continue for.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A limit on tokens per call, which bounds what each individual call costs.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Iteration and token caps bound the shape of the run without bounding its cost, since a step's expense varies with the context it carries. Accumulating spend and checking it against a ceiling is the direct control. Timeouts bound duration, which correlates with cost loosely at best.

stem: A planning step and an execution step are separated in an agentic design. What does that buy?

options.text: The planning can use a cheaper tier than the execution requires.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The execution can be parallelized, which the combined form prevents.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The plan can be reused across runs that share the same objective.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Making the plan an artifact creates a point where a human or a programmatic check can intervene before effects occur, which is the primary reason to split them. Parallelism, tier selection and reuse are all enabled to varying degrees and none is the reason the separation is recommended.

stem: An agent needs a working area for intermediate output that should not occupy its context. What supports that?

options.text: A separate conversation, in which the intermediate output is produced.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A longer context window, so the intermediate output fits alongside the work.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A summary step, which condenses the intermediate output before it is appended.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A file the agent writes to and reads back selectively when required.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Externalizing working state keeps the context focused on what the current step needs while preserving detail that can be retrieved on demand, and it survives the run if the file persists. Larger windows postpone the problem, summarizing loses detail irreversibly, and a separate conversation still has to hand results back.

stem: One worker in a parallel step fails and the orchestrator aborts the entire run. What should the design do instead?

options.text: Retry the failed worker until it succeeds, so the run completes fully.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Substitute a default result, and so the aggregation has something to work with.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Run an additional worker on the same subtask to replace the failed one.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Decide in advance which results are sufficient, and report what is missing.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Aborting discards work that succeeded and is rarely what the requester wants. Defining the sufficiency condition, and disclosing the gap in the output, makes partial success a designed outcome. Unbounded retries can hang the run, and substituting a default silently fabricates coverage.

stem: An agent encounters an ambiguity partway through a run. When should it stop and ask rather than proceed on an assumption?

options.text: Whenever an ambiguity arises, since proceeding on an assumption is never appropriate.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: When the assumption it would otherwise make cannot be recorded in the run's own output.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: When the ambiguity concerns the request itself rather than the material it is working from.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: When the ambiguity would change the effect of an action it is about to take.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Interruption has a cost, so the threshold is consequence: an ambiguity that changes which record is modified or which message is sent is worth a question, while one affecting only presentation is worth an assumption stated in the output. Asking at every ambiguity makes the agent unusable, and where the ambiguity originates does not determine what it costs to get wrong.

stem: Prompts are edited directly in the running system. What does that make impossible?

options.text: Testing a prompt against the cases it is genuinely expected to handle correctly.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Reviewing a proposed change before it affects the system's behaviour.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Rolling back to an earlier prompt once a problem has been identified.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Prompts are configuration that determines behaviour, and without versioning there is nothing to correlate a change in output with. stem: A user's message contains an instruction that contradicts the system prompt. What should the design assume?

options.text: That the model may follow either, so the constraint needs enforcement outside the prompt.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: That the contradiction is detected and reported rather than resolved silently.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: That the system prompt always prevails, since it really sits at a higher level of instruction.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: System-level instructions carry more weight and that is a tendency rather than a guarantee, which is exactly why a requirement that genuinely must hold is enforced in code, in tool authorization, or in a check on the output. stem: An input is genuinely ambiguous and the prompt does not address that case. What is the likely behaviour?

options.text: One reading is chosen and presented without the ambiguity being surfaced.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Both readings are produced, so the caller can select between them.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

stem: Structured tabular data is being supplied to the model as flowing prose. What does that cost?

options.text: Accuracy only, since in fact the values themselves are unchanged by the formatting.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Tokens and clarity, since the structure has to be reconstructed from the text.

options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Structure is information, and expressing rows and columns as sentences both inflates the token count and forces the model to recover relationships that a table states directly. stem: Examples are selected for each request based on similarity to the input. What is the trade-off against a fixed set?

options.text: Relevance improves and the prefix varies, so caching of that section is lost.

options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Dynamically chosen examples are more relevant to each case and they change the prompt on every request, which means that portion can no longer form part of a cached prefix. stem: An output must not exceed a length and instructions to be concise are not holding. What is more reliable?

options.text: Asking for the output to be revised down after it has been produced.

options.text: Providing examples at the target length, so the pattern is demonstrated.

explanation: A token limit is enforced by the decoder rather than interpreted, which makes it the mechanism when a ceiling genuinely must hold, with truncation detected via the stop reason. stem: A tool call hangs and the agent's loop waits indefinitely. What is missing?

options.text: A limit on iterations, which bounds how long the loop may continue.

options.text: A timeout on the tool, after which a failure is returned to the model.

options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: The application executes tools, so bounding how long it waits is its responsibility, and returning a structured failure lets the model decide how to proceed. stem: A tool can return either a complete result or a partial one when its source is slow. What should it do?

options.text: Mark the field required and set additionalProperties to false, which switches on range checking for that whole object.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Enforce the numeric range in the application's own validation layer, because bounds are not part of what is enforced.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Move the bounds onto an enumeration of permitted values, which is the only construct that constrains a numeric field.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Schema enforcement covers types, enums, constants, unions, references and closed objects — but not numeric bounds, string length constraints, or recursive schemas. Bounds declared in the schema are simply not applied, so the range check belongs in your own validation layer. Nothing about marking fields required activates it.

stem: A team sets strict mode on a tool so its arguments validate exactly, but the tool definition is rejected. Their schema declares an object with typed properties and nothing further. What is missing?

options.text: Strict mode requires the flag to be placed inside tool_choice rather than at the top level of the tool definition itself.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Strict mode requires every property to carry a description, which is what the validator uses when it binds the values.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Strict mode requires the tool to be forced through a named tool_choice, because it cannot operate under automatic choice.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Strict mode requires the schema to close the object with additionalProperties false and to list its required properties.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Strict argument validation needs a fully closed schema: additionalProperties set to false plus an explicit required list. The flag itself is a top-level field on the tool definition, which is a common misplacement — putting it inside tool_choice is a different parameter entirely. Descriptions help selection quality but are not a validation prerequisite.

stem: A reliability review asks which HTTP failures a worker should retry on its own and which it should surface immediately. Which split is correct?

options.text: Retry 429, 500 and 529; surface 400, 401, 403, 404 and 413, each describing a request the client has to change.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Retry 429 alone and surface every 5xx, since a fault on the server side persists until the provider has resolved it.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Retry 400, 429 and 500; surface 401, 403, 404 and 413, on the grounds that only credential faults need a human.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Retry every 4xx once and every 5xx three times, because client-side errors are frequently caused by transient state.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: The split is whether the request could succeed unchanged. Rate limiting and server-side faults are transient, so they are retried with exponential backoff and jitter. Malformed bodies, bad credentials, insufficient permission and oversized payloads all describe something the client must fix, and retrying them merely reproduces the same failure at a slower cadence.

stem: A pipeline joins batch results to its input list by position and finds records attributed to the wrong source document. What is the correct join key?

options.text: The index of each result within the returned page, which the service preserves for every successfully processed item.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The custom identifier assigned to each request at submission, because results are returned in no guaranteed order.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The message identifier on each returned message, which the service allocates sequentially as requests are accepted.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The request identifier in each result's response headers, which the service derives from the submission order it saw.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Batch results come back in arbitrary order, so any positional join is a latent data-corruption bug that surfaces only once ordering happens to differ. The custom identifier supplied with each request exists precisely to correlate a result with its input, and it is the only field guaranteed to do so.

stem: A workload occasionally returns a stop reason of refusal. The client currently treats that like a transient failure and retries the identical request up to five times. What should it do instead?

options.text: Strip the system prompt and retry, since standing behavioral instructions are the usual trigger for a refusal.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Retry once with a raised output cap, because refusals are most often a truncation artifact on a longer response.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Retry against a larger model tier, because refusal thresholds are calibrated separately at each model size point.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Surface the refusal rather than retrying, since an unchanged prompt will simply be declined the same way again.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: A refusal is a deliberate outcome, not a transient fault. Retrying the same input burns quota to receive the same answer. Surface it to the caller and inspect any stop details available; if the workload legitimately needs different handling, the prompt or the task framing has to change, not the retry count.

stem: A team caches a large system prompt. Cache reads look healthy for sessions with a fixed tool set, but fall to zero for users whose enabled tools vary from session to session. Why?

options.text: Tool definitions render after the messages, and anything appearing beyond a breakpoint invalidates it on the next write.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Tool definitions render ahead of the system prompt, so a differing tool set changes the prefix before the cached block.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Cache entries are scoped per tool, so any request that declares more than a single tool bypasses the cache entirely.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A cache breakpoint cannot be attached to a system prompt while tools are present, so the marker is silently discarded.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Caching is a byte-exact prefix match, and the render order is tools, then system, then messages. Anything varying in the tool set changes bytes at the very front of the prefix and invalidates everything after it, including a system prompt that is itself identical. Per-user tool sets are one of the most common silent cache killers.

stem: After enabling caching, a dashboard shows per-request input tokens dropping by ninety percent and the team reports a matching cost reduction. The meter reads the input token field only. What is wrong with that figure?

options.text: That field excludes the system prompt, which is billed separately and is usually the largest part of any request.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: That field is computed before caching is applied, so it always reflects what the request would have cost uncached.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: That field counts tokens rather than billing units, and cached tokens convert at a different rate per billing unit.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: That field counts only the uncached remainder, so cache creation and cache read tokens are missing from the total.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Total prompt size is the input tokens plus cache creation tokens plus cache read tokens. Reading the first field alone makes a well-cached workload look almost free, because the cached bulk has moved into fields the meter is ignoring. Cached reads are cheap but not free, and cache writes cost more than base input.

stem: A support tool sees bursts of three or four requests against the same prefix, separated by quiet gaps of roughly twenty minutes. Which caching configuration fits best?

options.text: No caching at all, since a prefix reused only three or four times cannot recover either of the write multipliers.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The shorter-lived entry, whose lower write multiplier pays for itself within the first two calls of every burst.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The longer-lived cache entry, which costs more on write but still holds across the twenty-minute quiet periods.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The shorter-lived entry plus a synthetic keep-alive request each minute, holding the entry open between bursts.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: The shorter-lived entry expires long before the next burst arrives, so every burst pays a fresh write and the reads never accumulate. The longer-lived entry has a higher write multiplier that needs roughly three requests to pay off — which a burst of three or four supplies — and it survives the gap. Synthetic keep-alives spend real tokens to avoid a write, which rarely nets out.

stem: A developer attaches a cache breakpoint to a four-hundred-token system prompt, sees no error, and finds cache creation tokens sitting at zero on every request. What explains it?

options.text: A breakpoint placed on the system prompt needs a second matching breakpoint on the final message before either one takes effect.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Cache creation is reported only on the request that first reads an entry, so the field is expected to remain at zero here.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The prefix falls below the minimum cacheable size, and requests under that floor are simply not cached rather than refused.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The prompt has to be supplied as a single string rather than a list of blocks before a breakpoint can attach to it at all.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: There is a model-dependent minimum cacheable prefix, on the order of a few thousand tokens. Below it, caching silently does not happen — no error, no warning, just zeros in the cache fields. This is a common source of confusion because the request looks correctly configured and behaves normally in every other respect.

stem: A router sends easy traffic to a small tier and hard traffic to a large one, with both sharing the same long cached instruction prefix. Cache reads land far below what the team projected. Why?

options.text: The classifier call sits between the cached requests and evicts the entry each time it runs against the small tier.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Routed requests arrive out of order, and an entry is reused only when consecutive requests happen to share a prefix.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A prefix may be cached for one model at a time, and whichever tier called most recently takes ownership of it.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Cache entries are scoped to a specific model, so each tier warms and then maintains an entirely separate entry.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Caches are model-scoped. A prefix cached against the small tier does nothing for a request routed to the large tier, so a two-tier design maintains two independent caches and each tier only accrues reads in proportion to its own share of traffic. Nothing evicts anything; the entries simply never overlap.

stem: A budgeting service sizes requests with a tokenizer borrowed from a different vendor and consistently under-provisions on code-heavy inputs. What is the correct instrument?

options.text: The platform's own token-counting call, issued against the exact model the request will subsequently be sent to.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The input token figure from a discarded trial request, which is exact although it costs an extra round trip first.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A character count divided by four, which is stable enough for budgeting once a reasonable safety margin is added.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The other vendor's tokenizer with a fixed correction factor applied to code and to non-English input specifically.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: A different vendor's tokenizer materially undercounts, and the error is worst on exactly the code and non-English text this service handles. The token-counting call is exact and model-specific, which matters because different models tokenize differently. A correction factor is a guess layered on a mismatch, and a discarded trial request pays real money for a number available for free.

stem: A classify-then-route design uses the large tier as its classifier and lets that call write a short justification before emitting its label. Realized savings land far below projection. Which correction pair is right?

options.text: Move the classifier to the cheapest tier and route ambiguous cases downward, so the large tier handles less traffic.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Keep the classifier tier but cache its prompt, so the repeated classification calls bill at the cached input rate.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Move the classifier to the cheapest tier and cap its output to the bare label, so triage stops dominating the bill.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Keep the classifier tier but batch the classification calls, so all triage runs overnight at the discounted rate.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: A router only pays off when triage is negligibly cheap: smallest tier, tiny output cap, label only. Justification text multiplies the output tokens of the call you make on every single request. The near-miss gets the tier right but inverts the routing bias — misrouting a hard case downward yields a confident wrong answer, so ambiguity should escalate, not descend. Caching and batching are real levers aimed at the wrong term.

stem: A team raises the effort setting to its highest level on a hard reasoning task while leaving the output cap at 1024 tokens. Responses now arrive truncated or nearly empty. What is happening?

options.text: High effort disables the output cap, so the response is instead trimmed by the transport layer partway through it.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Reasoning runs as a separate request whose result is spliced in, and that splice fails whenever the cap is small.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: High effort settings impose a minimum response length, and requests below that floor return a truncated placeholder.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Reasoning tokens draw from the same output budget, leaving very little of the cap available for the visible answer.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Thinking tokens count toward max_tokens. Turning effort up without raising the cap means reasoning consumes the budget and the answer gets whatever is left, which may be nothing. The fix is headroom: raise the cap when raising effort, and measure whether the extra depth is actually buying accuracy on this task.

stem: A model-selection layer holds a hardcoded table of context windows and per-feature support. Every platform update forces a code change and an emergency deploy. What is the better design?

options.text: Query the models endpoint at runtime for context windows, output caps and the per-feature support flags.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Read the limits from the usage object on each response, which reports the active model's window and its caps.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Derive each limit from the first error a model returns, then cache the discovered ceiling for later requests.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Pin every workload to a single model identifier indefinitely, so the table changes only when the team chooses.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: The models endpoint returns live capability data, so the selection layer discovers rather than assumes and stops needing a deploy every time the platform moves. Pinning forever trades one operational problem for permanent stagnation. Discovering limits by triggering errors is expensive and unreliable, and the usage object reports consumption, not capability.

stem: A team proposes an autonomous agent to reconcile and post month-end journal entries. The task is genuinely open-ended, high in value, and well within the model's ability. Which remaining criterion should block the design?

options.text: Viability: reconciliation is fundamentally arithmetic, which sits outside what a language model can attempt.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Value: month-end close runs only twelve times a year, so the per-run saving never repays the build effort.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Complexity: the steps are fully enumerable up front, so an agent adds nothing over a fixed sequential pipeline.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Recoverability: posted entries are costly to reverse, so a mistake cannot be caught and rolled back cheaply.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: The four criteria are complexity, value, viability, and cost of error — and all four have to hold. The stem grants the first three. Posting to a ledger is externally visible and expensive to unwind, so errors are not cheaply recoverable, which is exactly the criterion that fails. The usual remedy is not abandoning automation but placing a human checkpoint immediately before the irreversible step.

stem: An agent previously issued three tool calls in a single turn. After a refactor that returns each tool result in its own user message, it now issues one call per turn and throughput collapses. No errors appear anywhere. What happened?

options.text: Splitting results doubles the turn count, so the loop's iteration cap now truncates the run before it can finish.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Each user message resets the available tool set, so only the first tool stays usable for the remainder of the turn.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Results from one assistant turn all belong in a single user message, and splitting them suppresses parallel calls.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Parallel calls require an explicit flag to remain enabled, and the refactor removed the setting that turned it on.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Every tool_result block answering one assistant turn goes back in one user message. Splitting them across messages is accepted without error but reshapes the conversation the model learns from, and it quietly stops making parallel calls. The absence of an error is what makes this bug expensive: you lose throughput with nothing in the logs to explain it.

stem: A team wants an agent over their own custom tools, without hand-writing the request-execute-loop cycle, running on infrastructure they control. Which surface fits?

options.text: A hand-written loop over the messages endpoint, the only surface that will accept custom tool definitions.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The tool runner inside the regular SDK, which drives the loop over tools the team defines and hosts themselves.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, which supplies a loop plus built-in file, shell and search tools they have no use for.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Managed agents, which supply both the loop and a provider-hosted sandbox that this team would then have to run locally.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Two questions separate these surfaces: who supplies the harness, and who supplies the deployment. The tool runner supplies the harness for tools you define while you keep hosting — exactly the stated requirements. The Agent SDK is the coding-agent harness with built-in tools, managed agents move hosting to the provider, and every surface accepts custom tools.

stem: An agent drafts and dispatches supplier payment instructions. The team proposes gating dispatch on the model's own reported confidence. What is the flaw?

options.text: A confidently wrong output scores high, so the signal is weakest in exactly the cases the gate exists to stop.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Confidence scores are not available on the messages endpoint, so this gate cannot be built in the way described.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Confidence varies with prompt length, so the threshold would need recalibrating for each new supplier template.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Confidence is reported only after the tool call is issued, so the gate would fire once the payment had already left.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Self-reported confidence is not a control. It correlates with fluency rather than correctness, and a hallucinated payment instruction is typically expressed with complete assurance — which is the precise failure the gate was meant to intercept. Irreversible, externally visible, financially consequential actions need a human checkpoint, not a model-supplied score.

stem: One tool in an agent loop throws. The developer catches the exception, logs it, and continues the loop without appending anything for that call. The next request fails validation. Why?

options.text: The tool set has to be re-declared after any failure, since a tool that throws is dropped from the active set.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The exception has to be re-raised so the loop ends, because a partial turn cannot be continued once a tool fails.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Every tool use block needs a matching result, so the failure has to be returned as a result marked as an error.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The assistant turn has to be discarded and regenerated, because a turn with a failed call cannot be extended.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: The conversation must stay well-formed: each tool_use block requires a corresponding tool_result carrying the same identifier. A failed tool is reported by returning a result with the error flag set and a message describing the failure, which also lets the model recover or route around it. Swallowing the failure leaves an unanswered call and the next request is rejected.

stem: An agent must resume a multi-day investigation after its process restarts, with earlier findings intact. Which mechanism actually delivers that?

options.text: A larger context window, which holds the entire investigation and removes the need for persistence at all.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A memory store, since it reads and writes files that persist beyond the lifetime of any single session.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Compaction, which summarizes earlier context server-side and restores that summary when the process returns.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Context editing, which prunes stale tool results so the remaining transcript stays small enough to reload.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Compaction and context editing both operate within a session and both vanish when the process does. Memory is the only one of the three that crosses sessions, because it persists to files. A larger window postpones the problem rather than solving it, and it does nothing at all once the process has exited.

stem: With compaction enabled, a long-running agent gradually loses track of decisions taken early in the session. The loop appends the assistant's extracted text string to history on each turn. What is the defect?

options.text: Compaction keeps only the most recent turns by design, so early decisions are expected to be dropped entirely.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The compaction blocks in each response are discarded, so the API has nothing to substitute for compacted history.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Compaction summaries are delivered out of band and must be fetched separately once a session crosses a threshold.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Compaction is disabled automatically once tool results dominate a transcript, and the loop never re-enables it.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: This is the append-the-full-content-list rule again, and it bites hardest here. The response carries compaction blocks that the API uses to stand in for compacted history on the next request. Extracting only the text string throws them away, so the conversation silently loses its compaction state and the early context it was meant to preserve.

stem: A drafting step and a critique step run inside the same conversation, and the critique almost always approves the draft. Which change most improves the catch rate?

options.text: Add a rule to the drafting prompt requiring at least one criticism, so the critique cannot approve the draft trivially.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Run the critique as a separate call with its own context and an explicit rubric, rather than inside the drafting thread.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Have the drafting call critique its own output twice, keeping the result only when both passes arrive at the very same verdict.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Raise the effort setting on the combined call, giving the critique more room to reason about the draft it produced.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: A critique sharing the generator's context inherits its reasoning and its blind spots, which is why self-review approves nearly everything. Separating the contexts and supplying an explicit rubric is what makes the evaluator-optimizer pattern work. Forcing a criticism produces a token objection rather than a real one, and more effort on a compromised setup deepens the same reasoning.

stem: An operator instruction has to be injected mid-session without invalidating a large cached prefix. Which mechanism fits, and what is its caveat?

options.text: An edit to the top-level system parameter, which is universally supported and also leaves the previously cached prefix intact.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A user message carrying a reserved prefix string, which the platform promotes to operator scope when it is received.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A tool definition holding the instruction, since tool definitions render first and are therefore outside the prefix.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A system-role entry within the messages array, which preserves the cached prefix but is supported only on some models.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: Editing the top-level system parameter changes bytes at the front of the prefix and invalidates the whole cache — which is exactly what the requirement rules out. A system-role entry inside messages arrives after the cached prefix and is the non-spoofable operator channel, at the cost of being model-gated: unsupported models reject it. Tools render first, so they are the most cache-sensitive place of all.

stem: A long conversation is approaching the context limit. A developer argues the platform will drop the oldest turns automatically once the ceiling is reached. Why is that wrong?

options.text: Eviction covers tool results but never dialogue turns, so a conversation dominated by chat is left unprotected.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The API is stateless and processes exactly what is sent, so exceeding the window is the caller's error to prevent.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Eviction happens only when compaction is enabled, and this conversation never explicitly turned that feature on.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Eviction is applied per model tier, and the smaller tiers in use here have opted out of automatic history management entirely.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: There is no automatic server-side eviction. The API is stateless: it receives exactly the history you send and will reject a request that exceeds the window. Managing the budget is the application's job, whether by summarizing, trimming, enabling compaction, editing stale tool results, or retrieving selectively.

stem: An ingestion path silently trims any document that will not fit and proceeds. Reviewers argue this is worse than failing outright. What is the strongest reason?

options.text: The result is produced from partial input while the requester believes the entire document was taken into account.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Trimming spends tokens on content that is then discarded, raising cost without improving the resulting answer.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Trimming removes the end of a document, and the answers being asked for are more often grounded in its concluding sections.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Trimming breaks prompt caching, because the truncation point shifts the prefix bytes on every new submission.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: An error is visible and can be handled; silent truncation produces a confident, well-formed answer based on data the user believes was considered, with nothing anywhere to signal the gap. The right behavior is to say the document does not fit and offer real options — chunk and synthesize, summarize section by section, or retrieve the relevant passages.

stem: A team already places its question after a long report, and still cannot tell whether a given answer is actually grounded in the source. What should they add?

options.text: A requirement that every claim cite the passage it rests on, so a reviewer can check the grounding directly.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: A stricter output schema, which constrains the shape of each claim and thereby constrains its factual basis.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A lower effort setting, which shortens answers and so reduces the room available for ungrounded assertions.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A second pass asking the model to rate its own confidence in each claim it produced during the first pass.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Asking for grounded citations makes each claim checkable against the source, which converts an unverifiable summary into something a reviewer can audit in seconds. Self-rated confidence is unreliable in exactly the ungrounded cases that matter. A schema constrains structure, not truth, and shorter answers are not more grounded ones.

stem: A sixty-page contract fits comfortably inside the model's context window, and the team asks eight questions about it during one session. What is the appropriate handling?

options.text: Index it into a retrieval store and inject only matching passages, the general answer for any long document.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Send the document whole and cache the shared prefix, since chunking adds complexity the size does not warrant.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Split it across eight requests so each question carries only the pages a reviewer judged relevant to it.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Chunk it into sections and run map-reduce, because multi-question sessions benefit from per-section summaries.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Check whether it fits before engineering around a limit that is not binding. It does fit, and it repeats across eight calls, which makes caching the shared prefix the whole answer. Chunking and retrieval are the tools for documents that genuinely exceed the window, and applying them here buys complexity and a risk of missing cross-section context for nothing.

stem: A prompt currently holds the assistant persona, the tool trigger rules, and the customer's message all inside one long user turn. Which reorganization is correct?

options.text: Persona and trigger conditions both move to system, with tool descriptions kept minimal in order to save tokens.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Persona moves into the tool descriptions and the rules into the user turn, so each travels with what it governs.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Persona and standing rules move to system, trigger conditions move into the tool descriptions, data stays as data.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: All three move into the system parameter, so that the entire instruction set stays stable and remains cacheable as one prefix.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Each kind of content has a home: durable role and behavior in system, capabilities and their trigger conditions in the tool descriptions, and the volatile task and its data in the user turn. That split also keeps the stable part cacheable and keeps untrusted data clearly separated from instructions. Trigger conditions specifically belong in descriptions, since that is what the model reads when deciding to call a tool.

stem: A team defines a custom tool named bash for their own restricted command runner. Behavior becomes inconsistent and none of the built-in semantics apply. What is the issue?

options.text: Command-runner tools have to declare a schema-less type, and supplying any name overrides the built-in definition.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The custom tool shadows the platform tool only when both are declared, so declaring just one of them is always safe.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The name collides with a platform-defined tool, so the definition creates a different tool with no built-in behavior.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Custom names may not reuse any platform tool name, so the definition is rejected outright before the request is ever served.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Platform-defined tools like bash and the text editor are declared by type and name, with their input schema built into the model. Defining a custom tool that merely happens to share the name produces a different tool that looks similar and behaves differently, with none of the built-in handling. Pick a distinct name, or declare the real tool properly.

stem: A developer declares web search and code execution, then writes handlers for both and waits for tool use blocks that never arrive. What is the correct model?

options.text: Both execute on the provider's infrastructure, and their results return inside the same response with no client loop.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Web search runs server-side while code execution needs a client handler, so only one of the two handlers is wasted.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Both execute on the provider's infrastructure, but each result still has to be acknowledged with an empty result block.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Both need client handlers, but only once the beta header that enables client-side execution is added to the request.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Server-side tools — web search, web fetch, code execution, tool search — run on the provider's infrastructure and return their results as content blocks in the same response. There is no tool_use block to intercept and no loop to write. Client-side tools are the ones needing your execution loop: bash, the text editor, and memory.

stem: A research agent occasionally reports that no results were found for queries that plainly have results. The client wraps every call in exception handling and catches nothing. Where should it look?

options.text: The retry log, since the client's own automatic retry will already have substituted an empty placeholder for the failed search.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The returned result block itself, since a failed server-side search arrives as an error payload rather than an exception.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: The rate-limit headers, since a throttled search returns an empty result set with no other signal available to a caller.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The stop reason, since a failed server-side tool ends the turn with a distinct value the client is not branching on.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: A failed server-side tool call returns HTTP 200 with a result block whose content is an error object. Nothing raises, so exception handling never fires and a failed search is indistinguishable from an empty one unless the block itself is inspected. This is why treating server-tool results as always-successful is a real reliability bug.

stem: A first MCP integration is rejected with a validation error. The request declares the server's type, name and URL, and nothing else was changed. What is missing?

options.text: A tool filter listing which of the server's tools to expose, since the complete set is never mounted by default.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A credentials block on the server declaration, because a server cannot be reached without an inline access token.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A transport field distinguishing local from remote servers, which is required whenever a URL is being supplied.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A toolset entry in the tools array naming that same server, which every declared server has to be paired with.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: The MCP connector takes two parameters that always travel together: the server declaration and a matching toolset entry in tools whose server name matches. Declaring a server alone is a validation error. Credentials specifically do not belong in the declaration — that is the point of attaching them separately at session time.

stem: A reusable agent definition connects to a third-party MCP server. Where should that server's credential live so a prompt-injected run cannot read it?

options.text: In the agent's memory directory, which is scoped to that session and cleared once the session is torn down.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: In the agent definition's server declaration, which is stored server-side and never rendered into the context.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: In the system prompt behind a placeholder token that the harness substitutes just before the model reads it.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: In a separate vault attached at session time, with the secret injected after the request has left the sandbox.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: The architectural answer is to put the secret somewhere the model cannot reach: a vault attached at session time, substituted by a proxy after the request leaves the sandbox. Code running in the sandbox then cannot read or exfiltrate it even under successful injection. Every other option places a live secret inside model-readable or persisted context, and memory is the worst because it replays into future sessions.

stem: An agent currently sends outbound notifications through a general shell tool. Security asks for per-recipient approval. What is the right change?

options.text: Filter the shell tool's command strings for the send binary, prompting the operator whenever one is detected.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Promote sending to a dedicated tool with typed arguments, giving the harness a specific place to gate each call.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Add a system prompt rule requiring the agent to request approval before it composes any notification command.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Move the shell tool behind a slower approval queue, so every command rather than just notifications is reviewed.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: A shell tool hands the harness one opaque string for every action, which is why it is hard to gate. Promoting the action to a dedicated tool gives you typed arguments — including the recipient — that a gate, an audit log, or a UI can act on. Prompt rules are guidance, not enforcement; string-matching commands is a blocklist that quoting and pipelines defeat; and gating everything trades the problem for an unusable agent.

stem: A team argues that placing a third-party key in the system prompt is safe because the prompt is never shown to users. Why is it still a disclosure?

options.text: Prompts persist into session history and summaries, and sit inside context an injected instruction can ask for.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Prompts are logged by default at the provider and then retained well beyond the customer's own stated retention window.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Prompts are shared across tenants on a given model, so another customer's session may render the same prefix.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Prompts are transmitted without encryption, exposing the key to any intermediary sitting on the network path.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: A secret in the system prompt is durably stored: it lives in session event history, comes back from list endpoints, and is carried forward into compaction summaries. It is also inside the context window, which means an injected instruction can simply ask the model to repeat it. Keep credentials host-side or in a vault, where the model only ever sees a tool's result.

stem: An agent reads user-supplied pages and can write into a ticketing system. The team's entire defence is a blocklist of injection phrases. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: A blocklist adds latency proportional to page size, which becomes the binding constraint on a page-heavy workload.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A blocklist runs before retrieval, and injected instructions appear afterwards where the scanner cannot inspect them.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: An attacker can rephrase, translate or split the payload, so the list is unbounded and cannot be the primary control.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: A blocklist inspects only text, and injected instructions are usually delivered as images the scanner will skip past.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Phrase detection is an unbounded blocklist against an adversary who can rewrite freely, so it is a useful layer and never the control you build on. The durable defences are architectural: least privilege on the tool set, human approval before anything irreversible, credentials the model cannot read, and validation of side-effecting arguments in your own code. Assume injection sometimes succeeds and design so it does not matter.

stem: A file tool receives paths chosen by the model. The handler rejects any path containing a double-dot sequence before opening it. What does this miss?

options.text: Symlinks, absolute paths and encoded traversal, which can resolve outside the root without that sequence appearing.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: Relative paths, which the handler ought to reject outright because only absolute paths can be verified reliably.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Long paths, which some filesystems will truncate before the check runs, leaving the opened path different from the checked one.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Case differences, which let the same directory be addressed under a name the substring check fails to recognize.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Substring checks are a blocklist over an infinite input space. The correct approach is to resolve the model-supplied path to its canonical form and then verify that the result is still inside your project root — which catches symlink escapes, absolute paths, and percent- or unicode-encoded traversal alike. Never pass the raw path through to the filesystem.

stem: A multi-tenant assistant gives every session the same memory directory. Given the reference implementations, what is the concrete risk?

options.text: They version every file, so one tenant's rollback silently reverts edits other tenants made to the same file.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: They cap total directory size, so one heavy tenant can exhaust the shared quota and stall all the other tenants.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: They serialize writes globally, so concurrent sessions will block one another whenever memory is being written to at all.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: They ship no access control, so one tenant's stored notes can be read straight back into another tenant's session.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: The reference memory implementations have no built-in access control — they are a storage backend behind a directory, and whoever mounts it reads everything in it. In a multi-tenant system that is a cross-tenant data leak, so per-user directories plus the same canonical path validation you apply to any file tool are mandatory rather than optional.

stem: A team has a long, detailed release-checklist procedure used perhaps twice a month. Placing it in project memory bloats every session. What fits better?

options.text: A skill, which packages the procedure and is loaded on demand only when the task at hand actually calls for it.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

options.text: A slash command, the only mechanism able to carry instructions longer than project memory is permitted to hold.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A hook, which injects the procedure into the session automatically just before the first tool call is made.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: A subagent, which holds the procedure in a separate context and is invoked automatically whenever a session begins.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

explanation: Project memory is always loaded, which is right for universal conventions and wrong for a bulky procedure used twice a month. Skills exist for exactly that: packaged instructions for a recurring task, pulled in on demand when relevant. Hooks enforce policy on lifecycle events, subagents scope a delegated task, and neither is a mechanism for conditional instruction loading.

stem: A platform team wants a coding agent with built-in file, shell and search tools, running inside their own continuous integration, driven by a prompt and options rather than an interactive terminal. Which surface is it?

options.text: The tool runner in the regular SDK, which supplies the same built-in file and shell tools without a terminal.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The Claude Code desktop application, driven headlessly by scripting its interface from the pipeline runner.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: Managed agents, which run the same coding harness inside a provider-hosted sandbox reachable from a pipeline.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, which packages that harness and its built-in tools as a library they host themselves.
options.why: Marked correct in the imported set's answer key.

explanation: The Agent SDK is Claude Code packaged as a library: the coding-agent harness plus built-in file, shell, search and web tools, driven by a prompt and options, hosted wherever you run it. The tool runner is the near-miss — it automates the loop but ships no built-in tools, so the team would write every one. Managed agents move hosting to the provider, which the requirement rules out.

stem: A team needs to grade open-ended summary quality at scale, and plans to have the generating call score its own output against a rubric. What is the flaw, and the fix?

options.text: Rubrics cannot apply to open-ended text, so replace the rubric with exact-match checks over required key phrases.
options.why: Not the keyed answer in the imported set; see the explanation.
